metadata.title: Adolescents’ transitions between different views on democracy: Examining individual-level moderators

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses two-wave longitudinal survey data collected from Czech high school students (T1: May/June 2014; T2: Nov/Dec 2015) with random cluster sampling of schools within four of 14 Czech regions. The analysis is conducted in Mplus using a “complex” option to account for classroom clustering when computing standard errors and model fit indices, but the manuscript does not report the use of any student-level sampling/survey weights (e.g., no W_* weight variables are named). Because the dependent variables are latent class memberships and transitions estimated via LCA/LTA (not achievement PVs), there is no plausible-values weighting step. Therefore, the weighting approach is limited to cluster-robust standard errors via the complex design handling, and population-representativeness via explicit sampling weights cannot be confirmed from the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the study does not analyze ILSA cognitive achievement scales with PVs; instead, it models adolescents’ agreement with democracy items using latent class and latent transition analysis. Missing data handling is implemented via full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) at the item level, which is a model-based approach rather than a single imputation or deletion strategy. This means missingness is handled within the likelihood estimation for the LCA/LTA models, consistent with the reported covariance coverage range.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample comprises 768 high school students who participated at both waves (T1 and T2) in the Czech Republic. Sampling was conducted in four out of 14 Czech regions using random cluster sampling of schools from an official Ministry of Education register; all ninth and tenth grade classrooms available at the time entered the study. At T1, 1137 students were sampled, and 768 participated at T2 (approximately two thirds), with attrition analyses indicating no substantial sociodemographic or key-variable differences between longitudinal participants and those excluded for participating only at T1. In the LCA/LTA estimation, occasional item-level missingness was handled using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) with reported item-level covariance coverage of 91–99%, and classroom clustering was accounted for using Mplus “complex” with classroom as a cluster variable.

main_findings.dataset_used: Longitudinal democracy views (Czech high school students), T1 (2014)–T2 (2015), 9th/10th grade
main_findings.target_variable: Latent transition from liberal to conventional view
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent transition probabilities (from liberal at T1): transitioning to conventional=0.13. In predictor models (Table 6), transitioning liberal→conventional vs staying liberal: social movement participation B=-0.34, OR=0.71, p<.01; standard political participation B=-0.25, OR=0.78, p<.05; community service B=-0.96, OR=0.38, p<.05. Conditional probabilities of conventional at T2 after liberal at T1: for lower (−1 SD) vs higher (+1 SD) participation, social movement 0.30 vs 0.03; standard political 0.31 vs 0.03; community service 0.24 vs 0.05. Additional analysis (Latent transition from liberal to majority-oriented view): Latent transition probabilities (from liberal at T1): probability of staying liberal=0.61; transitioning to majority-oriented=0.26; transitioning to conventional=0.13. In predictor models (Table 6), transitioning liberal→majority-oriented vs staying liberal: gender (female) B=-1.09, OR=0.34, p<.01; institutional trust B=-1.36, OR=0.26, p<.01. Conditional probabilities: majority-oriented at T2 after liberal at T1 was 0.40 for males vs 0.20 for females; 0.42 for adolescents with lower trust (−1 SD) vs 0.13 for higher trust (+1 SD). Additional analysis (Latent class membership: majority-oriented vs conventional vs liberal views on democracy): Latent class analysis selected a 3-class solution at both time points (Time 1: BIC=7254.42; Time 2: BIC=7152.92). Class counts (most likely membership): Time 1 majority-oriented 235 (31%), conventional 241 (31%), liberal 291 (38%); Time 2 majority-oriented 301 (39%), conventional 255 (33%), liberal 211 (28%). Between-class differences at T1: institutional trust F(2,755)=29.97, p<.01 (η2=0.07); right-wing authoritarianism F(2,729)=35.63, p<.01 (η2=0.09); social movement participation F(2,735)=5.07, p<.01 (η2=0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using longitudinal democracy-view data from Czech high school students and latent transition analysis, the study leveraged civic participation types to predict transitions from the liberal to the conventional view, finding that lower participation levels were associated with a higher likelihood of moving away from the liberal profile. This indicates that encouraging youth civic participation (including protest, formal political, and community service activities) may reduce the risk of adolescents adopting more restrictive, convention-focused democratic views, while causality cannot be inferred from the observational two-wave design.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes two waves of longitudinal data from 768 Czech high school students (T1: May/June 2014; T2: Nov/Dec 2015) to model adolescents’ democratic views as patterns across eight agreement items covering general democracy support, civil liberties, and majoritarianism/minority rights. Using latent class analysis and latent transition analysis in Mplus (with classroom clustering handled via the “complex” option), the authors selected a three-class typology at both time points: majority-oriented, conventional, and liberal. The liberal class was less stable (stay probability 0.61) than the other two (0.89 and 0.86), with transitions from liberal to majority-oriented (0.26) and to conventional (0.13). Predictors of transitions showed that males and adolescents with lower institutional trust were more likely to shift from liberal to majority-oriented, while lower civic participation predicted shifts from liberal to conventional. Missing item-level data were handled with full-information maximum likelihood (FIML), and the design is correlational (no causal identification).
